In the examples below primary stress is marked by ", and secondary stress by '. Polysyllabic words usually have one primary stress and, if more than three syllables long, a secondary stress. new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Ayta Abellen (catalog-all-2026-09-12) has an empty rule and there are no existing stress statements, so there is nothing to agree with or contradict. This work adds: stress is lexically marked on either the final or the penultimate syllable of roots, there is a primary/secondary distinction, and suffixation (-en/-an) shifts stress rightward. Together with the companion Phonological Statement (43454, p. 4: 'Stress in Ayta Abellen is not predictable') it supports filling the empty record with 'lexical (unpredictable) (contrastive, mobile under suffixation)'.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The manuscript does not state a placement rule in prose; it is a 4-page list of morphophonemic processes. What it shows: word stress is marked lexically on individual roots and falls on different syllables in different words (final in he'lep, ke'teb, le'pad, ta'nem, ka'lih, ha'bet, la'kew, ka'get, ha'liw, ba'bol, ta'pol, mabi'til; penult in a'koyna, 'habtan, 'mani, 'apat, 'anem), i.e. neither the ultima nor the penult is fixed; and stress shifts when suffixes -en/-an are added (ba'bol -> babo'len, ta'pol -> tapo'len, ha'liw -> hali'wen, kam'po -> nagkampo'an: the stress moves rightward onto the suffix / final syllable), while syncopated suffixed forms keep stress near the deleted vowel (ha'bet+-an -> 'habtan, ta'nem+-an -> tam'nan, ka'get+-en -> kad'ten). This is consistent with the explicit statement in the same author's companion 'Ayta Abellen Phonological Statement' (SIL LCA 43454, already held by the project in the same folder, p. 4 §1.2): 'Stress in Ayta Abellen is not predictable. There is primary stress, and secondary stress.. Suffixation seems to cause stress to shifts.' The lexical (unpredictable) reading for this work is an inference from its stress-marked data, not a quoted rule.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Footnote 7 (p. 2): 'The low stress marker marks secondary stress.' In a combined stress group the first word's primary stress is demoted to secondary: mabi'til + a'koyna => mabi,til a'koyna 'I'm hungry now' (§3.1). No rule for the position of secondary stress within a single word is given here (the companion statement 43454 p. 4 says words of more than three syllables usually carry a secondary stress).
new_statements.exceptions: Stress shift after affixation (§3.2): suffixes -en/-an attract the stress to the final syllable (babo'len, nagkampo'an, tapo'len, hali'wen). In forms with vowel deletion the stress lands on the syllable adjoining the deleted vowel ('habtan, tam'nan, kad'ten, kal'yen, lak'wen, mamal'an; §2.1, §5.2, §8). Footnotes 8-9 attribute the vowel-raising forms man'yepat, man'yenem to 'the northern dialect of Labney'. Long vowel replacing reduplication carries the stress on the second element: ba'bai + ba- =>,ba:ba'i 'pl. of female' (§7, fn. 17).
new_statements.identity_note: The work describes Ayta Abellen [abp] generally (the companion statement names the barrios and language assistants Leonardo Francisco and Rodante Capiendo); footnotes 8-9 of the morphophonemic findings mark two vowel-raising forms (man'yepat, man'yenem) as belonging to 'the northern dialect of Labney'. The 2009 SIL grammar held by the project uses the spelling 'Ayta Abenlen' for the same language.
